title: Influence of preheating on the hardfacing performance of quenched and tempered steels under dynamic loading
abstract: Abstract Hardfacing is commonly applied to the working surfaces of demolition shears manufactured from high-strength steel base materials. These components are subjected to substantial dynamic loading, which fundamentally influences their service life. However, such base materials typically require preheating prior to hardfacing to mitigate the formation of brittle martensite during cooling. This preheating process is technically demanding and entails additional production costs. This study examines the effect of preheating on the microstructure, hardness, and impact behavior of quenched and tempered (Q + T) high-strength steels (S690QL, S960QL, S1100QL) used as base materials for hardfacing in demolition shears operating under dynamic loads. Hardness mapping across the heat-affected zones revealed that the influence of preheating diminishes with increasing base material strength: S690QL showed significant hardening differences, S960QL moderate, and S1100QL minimal. SEM analyses confirmed that microstructural variations between preheated and non-preheated conditions were negligible. Instrumented Charpy impact tests demonstrated that preheating slightly increased impact force and energy in lower-strength steels, while its effect was marginal for higher-strength grades.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hardfacing is widely applied across various industrial sectors, including mechanical engineering, mining, agriculture, and the automotive industry, as it offers long-term cost savings and extends the service life of machines and tools. During the application of this technology, one, two, or three layers of filler material are deposited by welding onto the surface of a steel base material, selected in accordance with the operational requirements of the specific component [ 1 ,  2 ]. In a significant number of cases, a so-called butter layer is also applied, which promotes proper joining, helps prevent crack formation and deformation, and improves the service life of the hardfaced component [ 3 ,  4 ].

The use of high-strength steels as base materials has become increasingly common, particularly in applications subjected to higher mechanical loads [ 5 ]. This topic was originated mainly due to issues that arose during the production of demolition shears, where steels with progressively higher strength are used due to complex mechanical stresses. As essential tools in heavy industrial operations, demolition shears play a crucial role in the construction industry, vehicle dismantling, as well as recycling and processing activities. These high-performance, hydraulically operated tools are capable of efficiently and precisely cutting, breaking, or separating a wide range of materials such as concrete, iron, steel, and other metals generated during the working process. Consequently, they are exposed to complex loading conditions, including: quasi-static loading, dynamic loading, torsional and bending loads, fatigue loading. In this case of demolition shears, typically three hardfacing layer applied to ensure longer lifetime, and it also means that multiple heat cycles have effect to the base materials [ 6 ].

In the welding of high-strength steels, heat input plays a critical role [ 7 ,  8 ] for welding technology planning. Furthermore, the t 8/5  cooling time is one of the fundamental parameters that must be considered during welding process design [ 8 ,  9 ]. The t 8/5  time primarily depends on the welding parameters and the level of preheating. If the t 8/5  time is too short (e.g., less than 5 s), excessive martensite formation can occur in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), which typically results in brittleness [ 10 ,  11 ], whereas excessively long t 8/5  times can cause considerable softening due to tempering of martensite [ 12 ,  13 ]. Additionally, the alloying, the carbon equivalent and material thickness have also significant affect to the microstructure.

Numerous studies have measured the hardness profile within the HAZ [ 7 ,  12 ,  14 ], showing that certain subzones exhibit hardening, while others display softening. Schroeder et al. examined S690QL material and found significant hardening in the upper-critical heat-affected zone (UCHAZ) [ 15 ], while Mician et al. observed only minor hardening in higher strength materials (e.g. S1100QL) [ 16 ]. The most softened zone is typically the inter-critical heat-affected zone (ICHAZ) [ 16 ,  17 ], whereas the sub-critical heat-affected zone (SCHAZ) generally exhibits a lower degree of softening [ 13 ,  18 ].

Previous studies have shown that the HAZ in high-strength steels is often the critical region controlling impact performance. In S960QL, for example, welding simulations revealed that heterogeneous microstructures containing martensite islands in intercritical HAZ regions lead to a reduction in impact energy compared to the base material [ 9 ]. Similarly, investigations on welded S690QL joints identified softened HAZ zones and microstructural gradients that affect crack propagation paths and impact behaviour [ 19 ]. More recent work on high-strength steels demonstrated that multiple thermal cycles can significantly modify HAZ toughness, with some softened subzones even showing improved Charpy impact energy compared to the base material [ 20 ]. Under dynamic loading conditions, such as Charpy impact testing, these steels exhibit strain-rate-dependent behaviour linked to their heterogeneous microstructures. Experimental studies on S690QL and S960QL have shown that high strain rates promote strain localisation and reduce ductility, while microstructural features such as phase distribution and grain size govern the overall deformation and fracture response [ 21 ]. In particular, the existence of hard martensitic regions and softer ferritic zones leads to strain partitioning and local stress concentrations, which are key factors in crack initiation within the HAZ.

In fusion welding of ultra-high-strength steels (UHSS), preheating is generally required to avoid excessively rapid cooling of the weld metal, especially for components with larger wall thicknesses. However, a review of the literature reveals that some studies incorporated preheating during experimental investigations [ 22 ,  23 ], while others omitted it [ 10 ,  24 ]. The influence of preheating has been also investigated in relation residual stresses, and it indicates that residual stresses are higher without preheating than with preheating [ 25 ], which also increases the susceptibility to cracking.

However, the literature provides little evidence regarding how changes in preheating conditions affect resistance to dynamic loading. It can be inferred indirectly that hardfacing without preheating may lead to increased residual stress [ 26 ,  27 – 28 ], which could also influence resistance to dynamic loading. Since dynamic loads represent one of the primary stress conditions acting on demolition shears, investigating this aspect is well justified. Moreover, in manufacturing practice, preheating can be problematic and represents a significant cost factor; omitting it could therefore simplify production processes. Consequently, the lack of prior research and the industrial motivation have prompted this study, which aims to determine how preheating influences the resistance of high-strength steels to dynamic loading during hardfacing. Hardness mapping, microstructural analyses and impact testing were used to identify the differences. Based on the literature review, it became evident that steels of different strength grades respond differently to preheating; therefore, three types of base materials (S690QL, S960QL, and S1100QL) are examined within the framework of this research.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: For the experimental program, quenched and tempered high-strength structural steels with varying strength levels were utilized. The S690QL and S960QL grades, which are widely employed in the manufacture of demolition shears and represent two of the most commonly used high-strength steels, were selected as primary base materials. To extend the scope of the investigation and achieve a more comprehensive comparative analysis, the S1100QL grade was also included in the study. In most hardfacing applications, the deposition of an intermediate butter layer (BL) between the base material and the hardfacing alloy is critical to ensure proper metallurgical compatibility and to mitigate dilution effects. Accordingly, a butter layer was employed in this investigation. The butter layer consumable corresponded to grade G CrMo1Si, as specified by ISO 21,952-A, manufacturer Lincoln Electric, type LNM19. This material was selected owing to its favourable ductility, moderate strength, and cost-effectiveness. A single butter layer was deposited on all hardfaced specimens. The hardfacing material utilized in the study exhibits high wear resistance and elevated hardness, making it suitable for surface protection in abrasive environments. In accordance with EN 14,700, its classification is S Fe8, manufacturer Lincoln Electric, type Carbofil A600. For all specimens, three hardfacing layers were applied. The nominal chemical compositions of the materials employed are presented in Table  1 , while the principal mechanical properties of the base steels are summarized in Table  2 . The data reported in these tables are derived from the respective material certificates.

sections.heading: Welding circumstances
paragraphs: The experimental procedure started with the hardfacing of all three base materials. Hardfacing was performed using the Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) process with a Cloos welding robot to guarantee precise positioning and consistent results. Preheated and non-preheated specimens were made during the investigation. For the preheated specimens, a preheating temperature of 120 °C was applied. According to the EN 1011-2 standard, the recommended preheating temperature ranges from 100 °C to 125 °C, depending on the carbon equivalent, but only one temperature was chosen to ensure good comparability. This study is based on a real industrial welding application, in which a preheating temperature of 120 °C was used; therefore, the same temperature was selected here. The temperature of the non-preheated parts was 25 °C. The shielding gas composition was 80% Ar and 20% CO₂. The welding parameters, calculated heat input, and t 8/5  cooling time are listed in Table  3 .
Table 3 Welding parameters Welding current [A] Arc voltage [V] Welding speed [mm/min] Heat input [kJ/mm] t 8/5  (preheated) [s] t 8/5 (non-preheated) [s] 220 21.3 250 0.9 6.4 4.8
Identical welding parameters were maintained for all base materials to ensure comparability. The resulting hardfaced surfaces measured 100 mm × 150 mm in each case.

sections.heading: Testing circumstances
paragraphs: Cross-sections of the hardfaced specimens were prepared through sequential grinding and polishing, using a 3 μm diamond suspension. The polished surfaces were subsequently etched using a 2% nital solution for 8 s to reveal the microstructural features. These etched cross-sections were utilized for both macrostructural imaging and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of the base material. Detailed microstructural characterization was subsequently performed using a Hitachi TM-1000 SEM. Following the microscopic examinations, Vickers hardness testing was conducted on the prepared cross-sections using a Reicherter UH250 microhardness tester under a 100 N load. Indentations were applied automatically, while the diagonal lengths were measured manually, maintaining a uniform spacing of 0.5 mm between successive impressions. The obtained hardness values were compiled to generate hardness distribution maps between two fusion lines, as illustrated in Fig.  1 .
Fig. 1 Method of hardness map creation:  a  cross-section with indentations,  b  hardness map

Charpy impact test specimens were prepared from the hardfaced components to evaluate the influence of preheating on impact toughness. The specimens conformed to standard dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm, with the notch locations determined based on the penetration: specifically positioned at the middle of the penetration and at the midsection between the penetration boundaries, as illustrated in Fig.  2 . The specimen preparation process involved sequential cutting, milling, and grinding operations. In total, 60 specimens were fabricated from the hardfaced sections (five specimens for each experimental condition), along with 15 specimens extracted from the base material.

Fig. 2 Schematic representation of notch locations on the Charpy specimens:  a  notch at the middle of the penetration (specimen identification: weld),  b  notch between the penetrations (specimen identification: HAZ)

Instrumented Charpy impact tests were performed using a pendulum-type impact tester equipped with a force–time data acquisition system. The instrument continuously recorded 2,500 data points over a 5 ms interval via an oscilloscope, enabling high-resolution characterization of the impact event and precise determination of the peak force. All impact tests were conducted at a controlled test temperature of − 40 °C (strictly controlled by thermometer), with an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 22 °C.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: The hardness maps were recorded for all specimens - with and without preheating - according to the procedure described in Fig.  2 . Hardness measurements were carried out at identical positions in each case, enabling direct comparison of the obtained values. Through this comparison, it was possible to determine the extent to which the hardness changed as a result of omitting preheating. Figure  3  illustrates an example of the comparison of hardness maps, where Fig.  3 a represents the specimen without preheating, Fig.  3 b shows the preheated specimen, and Fig.  3 c depicts the difference between the two.
Fig. 3 S690QL hardness maps:  a  without preheating,  b  with preheating,  c  difference between preheated and not preheated

Hardness maps were generated for both the preheated and non-preheated specimens of each material, making it possible to determine the ΔHV 10  (deltaHV 10 ) maps. Figure  4  illustrates these maps for the different materials.
Fig. 4 Differences in hardness values (ΔHV 10  maps) between preheated and non-preheated specimens:  a  S690QL,  b  S960QL,  c  S1100QL

Figure  4 a shows that significant differences in hardness values occurred in the UCHAZ zone (ΔHV 10  127–151), while only negligible differences can be observed in the ICHAZ zone (ΔHV 10  14–27). The SCHAZ zone lies between these two regions, with hardness differences ranging from 34 to 54 HV 10 . In the areas between the fusion lines, the hardness variations are much more uniform, typically within the range of ΔHV 10  42–79. In all cases, the hardness values of the non-preheated specimens were higher than those of the preheated ones. For the S960QL material, the differences in hardness values were considerably smaller. In the UCHAZ zone, differences of 59–92 HV 10  were measured, while in the ICHAZ and SCHAZ regions, the ΔHV 10  ranged between 5 and 27. This result clearly indicates that the higher-strength S960QL is less sensitive to preheating compared to S690QL. The smallest hardness differences were observed for the S1100QL base material, typically ranging between 3 and 41 HV 10 . The hardness maps show that the variations are greater in the regions between the fusion zones than along the fusion lines.

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: SEM analysis allows for the identification and interpretation of microstructural constituents; however, it cannot provide 100% accuracy, nor does it quantify the proportion of the individual phases. For more precise results, EBSD and/or XRD analyses would be required, but these were not available within the scope of the study. The microstructural investigations were first carried out on the base materials, and the SEM images are presented in Fig.  5 .
Fig. 5 Microstructure of the base materials (SEM, magnification: 3000x):  a  S690QL,  b  S960QL,  c  S1100QL

The base materials exhibit microstructures composed of martensite (M), partially tempered martensite (PTM), bainite (B), and ferrite (F). SEM observations reveal that S690QL predominantly contains partially tempered martensite and ferrite, with only minor occurrences of martensite. This microstructural composition accounts for the lower hardness and strength of S690QL compared to the other investigated steels. In contrast, S960QL primarily contains partially tempered martensite with small traces of full martensite. S1100QL, on the other hand, mainly consists of martensite and tempered martensite, with a minor presence of bainite. Martensite forms by rapid quenching and exhibits a supersaturated body-centered tetragonal structure, resulting in very high hardness and strength but low toughness due to significant internal stresses. In this state, carbon is trapped in solid solution, and the microstructure typically appears as sharp laths or plates. Partially tempered martensite, in contrast, retains a predominantly martensitic structure that begins to decompose toward ferrite and carbide phases, reflecting the effects of tempering. During this process, carbon precipitates as fine carbides, reducing internal stresses and slightly lowering hardness while improving toughness and ductility. These microstructural characteristics are consistent with findings reported in the literature [ 29 ].

Since the greatest differences in hardness were observed in the regions subjected to a single thermal cycle, the microstructural analyses were performed only for the UCHAZ, ICHAZ, and SCHAZ zones. Figure  6  shows the microstructures of the HAZ regions for the S690QL base material, comparing the preheated and non-preheated conditions.

Fig. 6 Comparison of HAZ subzones on S690QL (SEM, magnification: 3000x):  a  preheated UCHAZ,  b  non-preheated UCHAZ,  c  preheated ICHAZ,  d  non-preheated ICHAZ,  e  preheated SCHAZ,  f  non-preheated SCHAZ

In the case of S690QL, the UCHAZ primarily consists of martensite and partially tempered martensite in both the preheated and non-preheated conditions. The microstructure is typically coarse-grained, which is characteristic of this zone [ 7 ,  11 ]. The ICHAZ exhibits a much more complex microstructure; in addition to martensite and partially tempered martensite, ferrite and bainite are also present in both conditions. The main difference can be observed in the grain size - the non-preheated specimen shows a finer grain structure. The SCHAZ has a similar composition, consisting of martensite, partially tempered martensite, and ferrite, resembling closely the microstructure of the base material.
Figure  7  presents the comparison between the preheated and non-preheated conditions for the S960QL base material.

Fig. 7 Comparison of HAZ subzones on S960QL (SEM, magnification: 3000x):  a  preheated UCHAZ,  b  non-preheated UCHAZ,  c  preheated ICHAZ,  d  non-preheated ICHAZ,  e  preheated SCHAZ,  f  non preheated SCHAZ

In the UCHAZ zone, the microstructure is not completely identical between the two conditions. While the preheated specimen primarily consists of partially tempered martensite, the non-preheated specimen also contains untempered martensite. The ICHAZ of this material also exhibits a complex structure, comprising martensite, tempered martensite, ferrite, and bainite, with various carbide precipitations observable in both cases. No significant differences are evident between the two micrographs. In the SCHAZ, martensite and partially tempered martensite are dominant in both conditions, with a small amount of ferrite appearing in the non-preheated specimen. The main difference lies in the grain size, as the preheated specimen exhibits considerably larger grains compared to the non-preheated one.

The HAZ microstructures of S1100QL are shown in Fig.  8 . The two UCHAZ zones are very similar, both consisting of partially tempered martensite and martensite. No significant variation in grain size can be observed. The ICHAZ is again complex, containing martensite, tempered martensite, bainite, and ferrite. Comparing the two images, the martensite content appears slightly higher in the non-preheated specimen, while the ferrite content is lower. This observation is consistent with the theory that regions transformed to austenite can form larger amounts of martensite during faster cooling. In the SCHAZ, the microstructure predominantly consists of partially tempered martensite and martensite, with a small amount of ferrite also present.

Fig. 8 Comparison of HAZ subzones on S1100QL (SEM, magnification: 3000x):  a  preheated UCHAZ,  b  non-preheated UCHAZ,  c  preheated ICHAZ,  d  non-preheated ICHAZ,  e  preheated SCHAZ,  f  non preheated SCHAZ

Overall, it can be concluded that the microstructures of the different heat-affected zone regions changed only slightly, if at all, as a result of omitting preheating. The difference between the preheated and non-preheated t 8/5  times is only 1.6 s, which means significant microstructural differences cannot be resulted. This statement come from the CCT curves of the S690QL, S960QL and S1100QL, which can be found on relevant studies [ 10 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 ]. The considerable hardness differences observed in the measurements could not be clearly identified in the microstructures of the various HAZ subzones, but deeper analyses can give more exact results.

SEM images of preheated and non-preheated specimens show complex microstructure in all cases, which can lead complicated fracture behavior due to differences on slip systems, dislocation density and strain concentration.

sections.heading: Impact test results
paragraphs: Charpy impact tests were performed on both the preheated and non-preheated specimens to assess the differences occurring under dynamic loading conditions. The tests were carried out using an instrumented impact tester, which allowed the determination of both the absorbed impact energy (KV) and the maximum impact force (F imp ). Since five specimens were tested for each condition, the results were averaged, and the standard deviation (SD) as well as the coefficient of standard deviation (SDc) were calculated. In addition, the percentage of energy required for crack initiation (W i ) and for crack propagation (W t ) was determined. The results are summarized in Table  4 .

The table includes the test results for both the preheated and non-preheated specimens, covering the fusion (weld) and intermediate (HAZ) regions. The S690QL base material exhibits high impact energy, while the maximum impact force is relatively low. The impact energy of hardfaced specimens is approximately half that of the base material (BM)in the case of S690QL, regardless of preheating. This indicates that the heat-affected zone and part of the butter layer exhibit inferior impact properties compared to the base material. Previous study has suggested that this significant reduction is primarily due to the thickness of the butter layer, while the heat-affected zone itself does not have a detrimental effect [ 34 ]. For the S690QL weld, the average KV values are nearly identical between the two conditions, although the preheated specimens show a noticeably larger scatter. In contrast, a significant difference can be observed in the F imp  values, with the preheated specimens exhibiting higher maximum impact forces. Accordingly, the W i  values are also higher, indicating that although the total absorbed energy is similar, the preheated specimens achieved this through higher forces - suggesting a slightly more brittle behavior. In the S690QL HAZ, similar KV results were obtained, and the F imp  values did not differ significantly either. This clearly demonstrates that preheating does not affect the dynamic behavior of the specimens in the HAZ region.

The S960QL base material displays much lower impact energy compared to S690QL, but with considerably higher maximum impact forces. The impact energy of the base material is, in most cases, less than half that of the hardfaced specimens. This suggests that the heat-affected zone and the butter layer can have a beneficial influence on impact properties. However, previous studies have shown that while the HAZ significantly improves impact energy, the butter layer has a detrimental effect [ 34 ]. For the S960QL welds, a pronounced difference in KV values was observed between the preheated and non-preheated conditions, with the preheated specimens performing better. Similarly, the F imp  values were also higher for the preheated welds. Interestingly, as in the case of S690QL, the scatter in the results was larger for the preheated specimens. In the HAZ of S960QL, no significant differences were observed in either KV or F imp . For all S960QL specimens, the W i  values were relatively low, indicating predominantly ductile behavior. As with S690QL, the omission of preheating did not cause notable changes in the dynamic behavior of the HAZ region.

The lowest impact energy values were obtained for the S1100QL material. The base material exhibited very low impact toughness, while the maximum impact force was the highest among all tested steels. In the weld region, the preheated specimens showed higher impact energy, but lower F imp  values. In the HAZ, this tendency was reversed: the non-preheated specimens achieved higher KV and correspondingly the highest F imp  values. The W i  values were approximately 50% for all S1100QL specimens, indicating more brittle fracture behavior than S690QL and S960QL. In percentage terms, preheating had the greatest relative influence for S1100QL; however, even in this case, no substantial differences were observed.

In the case of impact energy, the SD and SDc values are relatively high in all cases, but it is typical for impact testing, while in the case of impact forces, these values are low. Compared with the base materials SD and SDc values are same or better in the cases of hardfaced specimens.
Figure  9  presents the force–time curves recorded during the impact tests for the different material grades, comparing the preheated and non-preheated conditions in the weld region.
Fig. 9 Force - time curves of impact tests on weld location:  a  S690QL,  b  S960QL,  c  S1100QL

Figure  9 a shows a significant difference for the S690QL weld, which was already anticipated based on the measured values. Both crack initiation and propagation behavior differ markedly: the shape of the curve for the preheated specimen indicates a more brittle response, while the non-preheated specimen exhibits a more ductile behavior. This finding is particularly interesting, as the hardness measurements suggested that the more hardened, non-preheated specimens would behave in a more brittle manner. This result shows that same impact energy can be reached by different way: while in the case of non-preheated result the curve shows tough behaviour, the curve of preheated specimen shows more brittle behaviour with much higher impact force. This difference can be seen on the W i  and W t  values too. For the S960QL material (Fig.  9 (b)), the curves show minimal differences; only a slight drop is visible in the descending branch for the non-preheated specimen, which likely accounts for the somewhat lower impact energy observed. In the case of the S1100QL weld (Fig.  9 (c)), the curves are very similar for both conditions, each indicating predominantly brittle behavior.

Figure  10  presents the force–time curves recorded during the impact tests for the different material grades, comparing the preheated and non-preheated conditions in the complex heat-affected zone (HAZ).
Fig. 10 Force - time curves of impact tests on HAZ location:  a  S690QL,  b  S960QL,  c  S1100QL

For the S690QL HAZ (Fig.  10 (a)), very similar, ductile-type curves can be observed; the effect of preheating cannot be detected from the curves. In Fig.  10 b (S960QL HAZ), a slightly greater difference can be seen: although both curves exhibit distinctly ductile behavior, the curve of the preheated specimen clearly shows slower crack propagation compared to the non-preheated one. For the S1100QL HAZ, a minor difference is also noticeable — the non-preheated curve displays a higher force value than the preheated curve. This observation is consistent with the results presented in the table. Moreover, both curves suggest brittle behavior.

In the HAZ of high-strength steels such as S690QL, S960QL and S1100QL steels, the deformation mechanisms under Charpy impact loading are governed by the local microstructure (martensite, tempered martensite, ferrite) and the associated dislocation behavior. Under the high strain rate which is typical of Charpy tests, dislocation motion is time-limited, which suppresses recovery processes and promotes strain localisation [ 35 ]. In martensitic regions, the high initial dislocation density and lattice distortion restrict slip to fewer active systems, leading to rapid stress build-up. As a result, plastic deformation is highly localized, which act as preferential sites for crack initiation and propagation [ 36 ]. Tempered martensite typically shows a more balanced response. Carbide precipitation introduces barriers to dislocation motion, but also enables more stable dislocation interactions and strain hardening. This reduces localisation compared to martensite and improves impact energy by hindering crack propagation [ 37 ]. Ferritic regions with lower dislocation density and higher amount of slip systems, deform more uniformly. However, under dynamic loading, strain partitioning between soft ferrite and hard martensite leads to the accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations at phase boundaries, promoting local stress concentrations and interfacial damage initiation [ 38 ]. Overall, during Charpy impact, deformation is controlled by limited slip activity in martensite, more homogeneous plasticity in ferrite, and intermediate behaviour in tempered martensite. The heterogeneous HAZ microstructure therefore drives strain localisation at hard phases and phase boundaries, governing the impact toughness and fracture behaviour.

This study is limited to hardness tests, basic microstructural analyses and instrumented impact tests. These results clearly show the slight differences between the preheated and non-preheated specimens, but residual stresses are not considered directly, while it assumed that it has effect to the cracking mechanism [ 26 ,  27 – 28 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Based on the results of the conducted research, the following conclusions can be drawn:

By mapping the hardness distributions, the hardness profiles across the complete heat-affected zones could be compared. In the case of the S690QL base material, significant differences in hardness were observed between the preheated and non-preheated specimens. For S960QL, the differences were considerably smaller, while for S1100QL, the variations were practically negligible. This indicates that with increasing strength of Q + T base materials, the extent of HAZ hardening decreases. Microstructural analyses were performed for both preheated and non-preheated specimens. Based on the SEM images, no substantial microstructural changes were detected for any of the materials. This observation also holds true for cases where more pronounced hardness differences were measured (e.g., S690QL UCHAZ). This result come from only SEM images, deeper microstructural analyses can give more precise results which can be correlated with the hardness maps. For the S690QL weld region, omitting preheating did not significantly affect the impact energy (KV), although the maximum impact force (F imp ) was lower. This suggests that in the preheated condition, the higher impact energy resulted from increased force (indicating more brittle behavior), whereas in the non-preheated condition, the higher ductility of the material contributed to the absorbed energy — a trend also supported by the force–time curves. No substantial differences were found in the S690QL HAZ region. For the S960QL weld, a notable difference in impact energy was observed between the preheated and non-preheated specimens, with the preheated condition showing higher KV and F imp  values. In the HAZ, however, no meaningful differences were observed in either parameter. The S1100QL specimens exhibited the lowest impact energy values overall. In the weld region, the preheated specimens demonstrated higher impact energy but lower F imp  values compared to the non-preheated ones. In the HAZ, this tendency was reversed — the non-preheated specimens showed higher KV and correspondingly higher F imp  values. Overall, the results indicate that the investigated high-strength steels are less sensitive to preheating during hardfacing, suggesting that hardfacing without preheating could reduce fabrication costs without compromising performance under dynamic service conditions. Additionally, the force-time curves can change significantly: higher impact force with more brittle behaviour can result same impact energy as lower impact force with tough behaviour. For future work, it would be of interest to perform impact tests at higher testing temperatures to further investigate the effect of preheating on the dynamic behavior of these high-strength steels. Besides, a deeper microstructural analyses and quantitative phase determination can give more precise support for the results.
